What is version control?

A version control system (VCS) is software that records changes to files over time, so
you can see who changed what and bring back any earlier version.

Career: your GitHub profile is a portfolio that recruiters look at.

   ⚠Git ≠ GitHub

   A common exam mistake is writing "GitHub is a version control system". Git is the
   version control system. GitHub is a hosting service built around Git. GitLab and
   Bitbucket are similar services.

question: Why can another developer's copy help recover a project when one computer is lost in a distributed VCS?

events.query: distributed VCS recover project another developer's copy

results.text:
Version control has grown up in three stages.

             Local VCS                       Centralized VCS                Distributed VCS  GIT

          💻 Your computer                    🖥 Central server                      ☁ GitHub
             🗄 versions                       🗄 all versions                      🗄 full copy

book the whole class must share: if the library is closed, nobody can study. The server
is a single point of failure.

3. Distributed VCS. Every developer has a complete copy of the project and its whole
history on their own computer. Examples: Git and Mercurial. Like every student owning
a full photocopy of the book: if one copy is lost, any other copy can replace it.

                                 Local                    Centralized               Distributed (Git)

Create a repository named exactly the same as your username (for example
    krish-patel/krish-patel         ) and tick Add a README file. Whatever you write in
   that README appears on your GitHub profile page, like a business card. The full
   steps are on the Labs page.

Unit 1 summary

   A version control system records every change: what, who, when and why.

   Local VCS keeps history on one machine; centralized VCS on one server;
   distributed VCS (Git) on every computer.

question: A developer fixes a bug and starts a feature during the same hour. How does the staging area help keep their commits separate?

results.text:
🧠The post office

   You write letters at your desk (working directory). You put the ones that are ready
   into an envelope (staging area); you don't have to send every letter you wrote.
   When you post the envelope (commit), it is sent and recorded.

Why have a staging area at all? Because real work is messy. You may fix a bug and
start a new feature in the same hour. Staging lets you commit them as two clean,
separate commits.

Checking where things are:                 git status

Notice that after    git add    , plain  git diff     shows nothing: the change moved to the
staging area. Each form of       diff    compares two of the three stages:

  Command                                Compares

   git diff                              working directory ↔ staging area (unstaged changes)

   git diff --staged                     staging area ↔ last commit (what you're about to
                                         commit)

$ git commit -m "Fix cart total for repeated items (fixes #3)"
  $ git push

When that commit reaches the default branch, GitHub closes issue #3 automatically.

If a teammate pushed before you, Git refuses your push. Never panic and never
   force it: run  git pull    , then   git push     again.

The daily loop

  💾   git commit -m     →      ☁   git push

Pull requests: proposing changes

A pull request (PR) says: "Here is my branch. Please review it and merge it into                main   ."
It is how professional teams merge work, because a teammate checks the code first.

staged   .
